summary: Design a browser history supporting visit, back(steps) and forward(steps).
mainInsight: Keep the pages in an array with a cursor. Visiting a new page truncates everything ahead of the cursor and adds the page; back/forward just move the cursor, clamped to the valid range.

approaches.name: Two stacks (back/forward)
approaches.summary: Move pages between back and forward stacks.

approaches.name: Array + cursor
approaches.summary: history list with cur and a valid length (or truncate with slicing).

personalSolution.approach: Array + cursor with a valid length
personalSolution.notes: Correct and O(1). Simplify back/forward with max/min clamping.

cards.answer: One array of pages with a cursor: visit truncates the forward history, back and forward move the cursor. Clue: It asks for a structure with visit, back and forward where a visit discards the forward pages, so keep one ordered list and the index of the current page.
keyPoints: It asks for a structure with visit, back and forward where a visit discards the forward pages, so keep one ordered list and the index of the current page.
cards.explanation: A cursor into one list gives constant-time moves, and visiting simply cuts the list at the cursor.

promptVariants: How do you model the browser tabs' history efficiently?
options: An array of visited pages plus a cursor index into it
A priority queue ordered by the time each page was visited
A hash set of visited pages with their visit counts
A trie of the page addresses to find the previous and next pages
cards.answer: An array of visited pages plus a cursor index into it
cards.explanation: Index arithmetic jumps any number of steps at once. (Array with a cursor: clamped moves)

promptVariants: What does visit do to the forward history?
Why is the forward history discarded on visit?
cards.answer: Visiting a new page from the middle of the history clears all pages ahead of the cursor (the forward history), because the browser branches to a new timeline. The new page is placed right after the cursor and becomes the last valid page.
cards.explanation: That is the part most implementations get wrong.

promptVariants: Time of back/forward with an array cursor: ___
What is the space cost and how does truncating by slicing compare with your 'valid length' trick?
How do slicing and a valid-length counter differ when truncating the forward history?
cards.answer: O(n) pages. Slicing (history = history[:cur + 1]) is simple but may copy O(n) on each visit; tracking a valid length overwrites in place at O(1) per visit.

promptVariants: Your back() uses two conditions `steps > validLen - 1 or steps > curr`. Simplify the cursor movement.
How do you clamp back and forward correctly?
cards.answer: Back is simply `self.curr = max(0, self.curr - steps)` and forward is `self.curr = min(self.validLen - 1, self.curr + steps)`. The first condition in your code is redundant because steps > curr already covers it.

promptVariants: After visit(a), visit(b), back(1), visit(c), what does forward(1) return?
options: It stays on c: visiting c cleared the forward history
It returns b, because b is still stored right after the cursor
It returns a, because forward moves back to the older page
It raises an error because forward history is empty
cards.answer: It stays on c: visiting c cleared the forward history
cards.explanation: Visiting c from a clears the forward history, so forward(1) cannot move and returns c. (It stays on c: the forward history was discarded)

incorrectOptionExplanations.It returns b, because b is still stored: b was discarded when visiting c.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It raises an error because forward histo: Forward is clamped, not an error.
